etymology: From Old French remembrer, from Latin rememorari — to call to mind again, from memor, mindful. The Hebrew zākar is not merely mental recall: when God remembers, He acts. He remembered Noah and made a wind to pass over the earth; He remembered Rachel and opened her womb; He remembered His covenant with Abraham and brought Israel out. To remember, in Scripture's idiom, is to turn attention into action on behalf of the one remembered.
biblical_def: Remembrance in Scripture is a covenant act on both sides. God remembers His covenant, and the remembering is His intervening — not the recovery of something He had mislaid, for He does not forget, but the appointed moment at which He moves on what He has promised. Israel, correspondingly, is commanded to remember, and the commands are the backbone of her obedience: “Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy” (Exo 20:8); remember that thou wast a bondman in Egypt; remember all the way which the LORD thy God led thee these forty years. The Preacher gives the command its most urgent form — “Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, while the evil days come not” (Ecc 12:1) — setting remembrance in the season when it is least felt to be necessary. The Psalmist turns the same duty inward and speaks to his own soul: “Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits” (Psa 103:2), which is the ordinary work of a believer preaching to himself against his own drift. And the Lord Jesus, on the night He was betrayed, gathered the whole doctrine into an ordinance: “this do in remembrance of me” (Luk 22:19). The supper exists because we forget, and it is not a bare exercise of memory but a proclamation — ye do shew the Lord's death till he come. The thief's plea on the cross is the shortest and best prayer in this vein: Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom.
webster_summary: To call to mind; in Scripture, when used of God, to act upon what He has promised, and when commanded of men, the deliberate keeping in view of God's works, benefits, and law — a duty because forgetfulness is the native motion of the fallen heart.
webster_full: REMEMBER, v.t. 1. To have in the mind an idea which had been in the mind before, and which recurs to the mind without effort.
2. To bear or keep in mind; to attend to. Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy. Exod. 20.
3. To preserve the memory of; to commemorate. This do in remembrance of me. Luke 22.
4. When spoken of God, to remember is to regard with favor and to act for the deliverance or blessing of the person. God remembered Noah. Gen. 8. God remembered Rachel. Gen. 30.
5. To remember against; to call to mind for punishment. Remember not against us former iniquities. Psalm 79.
scriptures: Ecclesiastes 12:1
Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, while the evil days come not, nor the years draw nigh, when thou shalt say, I have no pleasure in them;
Exodus 20:8
Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy.
Psalm 103:2
Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits:
Luke 22:19
And he took bread, and gave thanks, and brake it, and gave unto them, saying, This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me.
corruption_summary: The Lord's command to remember Him is reduced to a private act of recollection, so that the supper becomes a memory exercise performed by individuals rather than a covenant meal in which Christ is truly present to faith and His death is proclaimed by the church.
corruption_paragraphs: Bare memorialism takes in remembrance of me to mean that nothing occurs at the table except thinking. That underreads the Hebrew and Greek both. Remembrance in Scripture is never merely cognitive; the anamnēsis of the supper stands in the line of the passover, which Israel kept as a real participation in a real deliverance, so that each generation said the LORD brought us out. The Reformed confession holds what memorialism drops without adding what Rome invents: the elements remain bread and wine, no sacrifice is repeated, and yet the believer by faith truly feeds upon Christ crucified, who is really and spiritually present by His Spirit. The table gives what it signifies to those who receive it by faith.

The opposite corruption is to make remembrance a work. Where the frequency, posture, or feeling of the communicant is treated as what secures the benefit, the supper has been turned into a performance and the covenant has been read backwards. Scripture's order is that God remembers first — He remembered His holy promise, and Abraham His servant — and our remembering is response, not cause. This is also the answer to the anxious conscience that fears it has not remembered well enough at the table. The thief had no ordinance, no preparation, and no time; he asked only to be remembered, and the reply was that he would be in paradise that day.
roots_summary: Hebrew zākar joins memory to action, and gives the noun zikkārōn, a memorial. Greek mimnēskō is to be mindful; anamnēsis, a calling to mind, is the word in the institution of the supper.
roots_lines: Hebrew zākar (H2142) — to remember, to mark, to mention; some 233 occurrences. Of God it means to act on a promise; of men, to keep in view and obey.
Hebrew zikkārōn (H2146) — a memorial, a reminder; used of the stones out of Jordan, of the passover, and of the trumpets blown over the offerings.
Hebrew 'azkārâh (H234) — the memorial portion of the meat offering, burnt upon the altar as the part that brings the offerer to remembrance before God.
Greek mimnēskō (G3403) — to remind, to be mindful of; used of the Lord remembering His holy covenant (Luk 1:72) and of Peter remembering the word of Jesus.
Greek anamnēsis (G364) — a calling to mind, a remembrance; the word of Luk 22:19 and 1Co 11:24-25, and of the yearly remembrance again made of sins in Heb 10:3.
usage: Of God acting on His covenant: God remembered Noah (Gen 8:1); I will remember my covenant (Lev 26:42); he hath remembered his mercy (Luk 1:54).
Of commanded duty: remember the sabbath day (Exo 20:8); remember thy Creator in the days of thy youth (Ecc 12:1); remember Lot's wife (Luk 17:32).
Of the ordinance: this do in remembrance of me (Luk 22:19); Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom (Luk 23:42).

etymology: From Old English forgietan, the prefix for- carrying a privative or destructive force (as in forbid, forsake) joined to gietan, to get or grasp — so, literally, to lose one's grip on. The Hebrew shākach is used the same way, of letting a thing slip out of mind and therefore out of practice, and the Greek epilanthanomai is built on lanthānō, to escape notice — what is forgotten has slipped past the attention.
biblical_def: Forgetting in Scripture is rarely a failure of the memory and almost always a failure of the heart. Moses warns Israel not against poor recall but against prosperity: “Beware that thou forget not the LORD thy God, in not keeping his commandments” (Deu 8:11) — and the verse defines the sin, because forgetting God is not keeping His commandments. The context makes the danger plain: when thou hast eaten and art full, and hast built goodly houses and dwelt therein, then thine heart be lifted up and thou forget. Judgment follows the category: “The wicked shall be turned into hell, and all the nations that forget God” (Psa 9:17) — not the nations that blaspheme Him, but simply those that leave Him out. Against this stands the impossibility of God's forgetting His own, put in the tenderest terms Scripture has: “Can a woman forget her sucking child?…yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee” (Isa 49:15), followed by the graving of Zion on the palms of His hands. And the writer to the Hebrews applies the same assurance to service: “God is not unrighteous to forget your work and labour of love” (Heb 6:10). There is also a forgetting that is commanded and holy — forgetting those things which are behind, Paul reaches forth unto those things which are before — and a forgetting that belongs to God alone, for He says of the new covenant that He will remember their sin no more.
webster_summary: To lose from the mind, and in Scripture's idiom to lose from practice; the characteristic sin of the prosperous, defined by Moses as the not-keeping of God's commandments, and the one thing God declares He will not do toward His people or their labour of love.
webster_full: FORGET, v.t. 1. To lose the remembrance of; to let go from the memory.
2. To slight; to neglect. Can a woman forget her sucking child? Isa. 49.
3. In Scripture, to forget God is to cease to regard his commandments and his benefits; a sin most incident to those in prosperity. Beware that thou forget not the LORD thy God. Deut. 8.
4. Of God, to forget is to withhold favor, or in mercy to remember sin no more. Their sin will I remember no more. Jer. 31.
5. To forget one's self; to lose the recollection of what belongs to one's character and station; and hence to be carried into unbecoming conduct.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 8:11
Beware that thou forget not the LORD thy God, in not keeping his commandments, and his judgments, and his statutes, which I command thee this day:
Psalm 9:17
The wicked shall be turned into hell, and all the nations that forget God.
Isaiah 49:15
Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee.
Hebrews 6:10
For God is not unrighteous to forget your work and labour of love, which ye have shewed toward his name, in that ye have ministered to the saints, and do minister.
corruption_summary: Forgetting God is not treated as a sin at all in the modern conscience, since it involves no act; and where a nation quietly leaves God out of its reckoning, Psa 9:17 is precisely the verse being ignored.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern moral vocabulary is built almost entirely on acts and their consequences, which leaves it with no category for a sin of omission that feels like nothing. Yet Scripture names forgetting God as the road to judgment for whole nations, and Moses locates its cause not in hardship but in success: full barns, good houses, multiplied silver and gold, and then a lifted-up heart. A society may keep every outward decency and still be, in the exact sense of Psa 9:17, a nation that forgets God — and the mark of it is not open blasphemy but the quiet dropping of God from public reckoning as a subject that need not come up. Deu 8 makes the remedy as concrete as the danger: thou shalt remember the LORD thy God, for it is he that giveth thee power to get wealth.

There is also a therapeutic misuse of the biblical language of forgetting, which turns Paul's forgetting those things which are behind into a licence to bury sin without repentance and injury without reconciliation. Paul is describing the athlete's refusal to look back over his shoulder at attainments and failures alike while the race is still running; he is not counselling the suppression of what conscience has not dealt with. Scripture's way with the past is confession, restitution where it is owed, and forgiveness — after which the sin is genuinely gone, because God has said He will remember it no more. That is a divine act, not a technique, and no creature can perform it on himself.
roots_summary: Hebrew shākach is to forget, mislay, or ignore. Greek epilanthanomai is to let escape notice, and lēthē, forgetfulness, gives 2Pe 1:9 its picture of a man who has forgotten that he was purged from his old sins.
roots_lines: Hebrew shākach (H7911) — to forget, to ignore, to cease to care for; some 102 occurrences, including the sheaf forgotten in the field and left for the stranger (Deu 24:19).
Hebrew nāshâh (H5382) — to forget, to deprive of memory; the root behind the name Manasseh, God hath made me forget all my toil (Gen 41:51).
Greek epilanthanomai (G1950) — to forget, to neglect; used in Heb 6:10 of what God will not do, and in Heb 13:2 and 16 of what we must not — hospitality, and to do good and communicate.
Greek lēthē (G3024) — forgetfulness; the noun in 2Pe 1:9, having forgotten that he was purged from his old sins.
Greek eklanthanomai (G1585) — to forget utterly, to let slip entirely; used once, in Heb 12:5, ye have forgotten the exhortation which speaketh unto you as unto children.
usage: Of the sin of the prosperous: beware that thou forget not the LORD thy God (Deu 8:11); when thy herds and thy flocks multiply, then thine heart be lifted up (Deu 8:13-14).
Of national judgment: all the nations that forget God (Psa 9:17); my people have forgotten me days without number (Jer 2:32).
Of what God will not forget and what He will: yet will I not forget thee (Isa 49:15); God is not unrighteous to forget your work (Heb 6:10); their sin will I remember no more (Jer 31:34).

etymology: From Old English sēcan, common Germanic, cognate with Latin sagire, to perceive keenly — the root idea is tracking, following a scent. Hebrew has two words the Authorized Version renders alike: bāqash, to search for what is missing, and dārash, to enquire of, to consult, to resort to — the word used of enquiring of the LORD by a prophet. Seeking God in Scripture is therefore both a search and a consultation.
biblical_def: Seeking is the ordinary biblical name for the whole active side of religion, and Scripture presses it with promises attached. “Seek ye the LORD while he may be found, call ye upon him while he is near” (Isa 55:6) sets the duty inside a window that will close, and the next verse turns it into a call to repentance — let the wicked forsake his way. Amos reduces the whole prophetic message to four words: “Seek ye me, and ye shall live” (Amo 5:4). Jeremiah supplies the condition that governs every such promise: “ye shall seek me, and find me, when ye shall search for me with all your heart” (Jer 29:13) — the seeking that finds is whole-hearted, and a divided search is what fails, not an insufficiently clever one. The Lord Jesus then orders the whole life by it: “seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you” (Mat 6:33), where the priority is not a ranking of interests but a single governing pursuit that resolves the anxieties listed above it. Yet the doctrine has a foundation beneath it that Scripture is careful to lay: none seeketh after God, says Paul, quoting the psalm; the seeking creature is himself first sought, for the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost. The believer's seeking is real, commanded, and effortful, and it is the fruit of having been found.
webster_summary: To search for, and in Scripture to enquire of and resort to God; the commanded active side of religion, promised success on the condition of the whole heart, made the single governing priority by Christ, and grounded on His prior seeking of the lost.
webster_full: SEEK, v.t. 1. To go in search or quest of; to look for; to search for by going from place to place.
2. To inquire for; to ask for; to solicit. Seek ye the LORD while he may be found. Isa. 55.
3. To have recourse to; to resort to. In Scripture, to seek God is to have recourse to him by prayer and by his word, and to make his favor the chief object of pursuit.
4. To seek after; to make pursuit; to attempt to find or take. The Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost. Luke 19.
5. To seek to; to apply to; to have recourse to for counsel, as Saul sought to a familiar spirit, which the law had forbidden. 1 Sam. 28.
scriptures: Isaiah 55:6
Seek ye the LORD while he may be found, call ye upon him while he is near:
Jeremiah 29:13
And ye shall seek me, and find me, when ye shall search for me with all your heart.
Amos 5:4
For thus saith the LORD unto the house of Israel, Seek ye me, and ye shall live:
Matthew 6:33
But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.
corruption_summary: Seeking has been made the name of a permanent condition rather than a directed search — the “seeker” who is admired precisely for never arriving — which inverts a Bible in which seeking is commanded because finding is promised.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern religious ideal of the seeker prizes the search itself and treats arrival as a kind of intellectual bad manners: to have found is to have stopped thinking. Scripture knows nothing of this. Every biblical command to seek carries a promise of finding attached to it — seek, and ye shall find; ye shall seek me and find me; seek ye me, and ye shall live — and the one class of seekers the Lord rebukes is those who are ever learning and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth. The Bible's seeking has an object and an end. What it excludes is not settled conviction but the half-hearted search that Jer 29:13 anticipates, which fails on the condition of the whole heart rather than on the difficulty of the object.

A second corruption runs through church practice, where seeker became a category to be catered to, and services were reshaped to remove whatever an unconverted visitor might find strange — which in practice meant the law, the cross, sin, judgment, and the demand for repentance. The stated theory is that men are seeking God and need obstacles removed. Paul's theology is the reverse: there is none that seeketh after God, and what the natural man requires is not fewer obstacles but a new heart, which comes by the foolishness of preaching. Isa 55:6 remains the true evangelistic note, and it is urgent rather than accommodating: seek Him while he may be found, because there is a nearness that does not last.
roots_summary: Hebrew bāqash is to search for what is wanted; dārash is to enquire of, to consult, to resort to, and gives the noun midrash. Greek zēteō is to seek, and the compound ekzēteō intensifies it to seek out diligently.
roots_lines: Hebrew bāqash (H1245) — to seek, to search out, to require; some 225 occurrences, from seeking a lost thing to seeking the LORD's face.
Hebrew dārash (H1875) — to enquire, to consult, to resort to; the word for enquiring of the LORD, and also for the forbidden enquiry of familiar spirits.
Greek zēteō (G2212) — to seek, to desire, to require; the word of Mat 6:33 and of the woman seeking her lost piece of silver.
Greek ekzēteō (G1567) — to seek out earnestly; used in Heb 11:6, God is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him, and in Rom 3:11, there is none that seeketh after God.
Greek epizēteō (G1934) — to seek after, to crave; used of the Gentiles who seek after food and raiment (Mat 6:32) and of those who seek a sign.
usage: Of the commanded search with a promise: seek ye the LORD while he may be found (Isa 55:6); seek, and ye shall find (Mat 7:7).
Of the condition of the whole heart: when ye shall search for me with all your heart (Jer 29:13); with my whole heart have I sought thee (Psa 119:10).
Of Christ's prior seeking: the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost (Luk 19:10); there is none that seeketh after God (Rom 3:11).

etymology: From Old English findan, common Germanic, with an underlying sense of coming upon in the course of travelling — the same root gives German finden and is related to words for a path or journey. The Greek heuriskō is the verb behind Archimedes' reported cry and behind English heuristic; it carries the note of discovery, of a thing turning up to the one who was looking.
biblical_def: Finding in Scripture is the promised end of seeking, and it belongs to the vocabulary of grace more than to the vocabulary of achievement. The Lord attaches it to prayer as a plain guarantee: “Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you” (Mat 7:7), three imperatives with three promises, and the argument that follows is from lesser to greater — if evil men give good gifts to their children, how much more shall your Father. Wisdom makes the same promise in her own voice: “I love them that love me; and those that seek me early shall find me” (Pro 8:17). But the deepest use reverses the direction, and Scripture is emphatic about it. The parables of Luke 15 are three stories of finding in which the lost thing does no seeking at all: the shepherd goes after the sheep until he find it, and says, “Rejoice with me; for I have found my sheep which was lost” (Luk 15:6); the woman sweeps the house till she finds the coin; the father sees the son a great way off. The Lord states the doctrine plainly — the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost — and Andrew's report to his brother is the believer's ordinary form of it: “We have found the Messias” (Joh 1:41). Finally there is the great paradox by which the terms are set against each other: “whosoever will save his life shall lose it: and whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it” (Mat 16:25).
webster_summary: To come upon, to discover, to obtain; in Scripture the promised issue of seeking and asking, the shepherd's word over the recovered sheep, and the term of the Lord's paradox that a life is found only by being lost for His sake.
webster_full: FIND, v.t. 1. To meet or fall in with; to come to; to discover by the eye or by the intellect.
2. To obtain, as by seeking or searching. Seek, and ye shall find. Matt. 7.
3. To discover by experience or trial. Ye shall find rest unto your souls. Matt. 11.
4. To recover that which was lost. I have found my sheep which was lost. Luke 15.
5. To find favor; to be graciously received; a frequent Hebrew idiom. Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD. Gen. 6.
scriptures: Matthew 7:7
Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you:
Proverbs 8:17
I love them that love me; and those that seek me early shall find me.
Luke 15:6
And when he cometh home, he calleth together his friends and neighbours, saying unto them, Rejoice with me; for I have found my sheep which was lost.
Matthew 16:25
For whosoever will save his life shall lose it: and whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it.
corruption_summary: The language of finding has been turned inward — finding oneself, finding one's truth — so that the object of the search becomes the searcher, which is the precise inversion of a Gospel in which the lost are found by Another.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning idiom of the age is self-discovery: the authentic self is said to lie buried under expectation and obligation, and the great work of a life is to find it and be true to it. Scripture's diagnosis of the buried self is different. What lies underneath, on examination, is a heart deceitful above all things and desperately wicked; the self is not a treasure awaiting excavation but the very thing that requires renewal. Hence the Lord's deliberate use of the same verb against the instinct: he that findeth his life shall lose it, and he that loseth his life for my sake shall find it. The promise is not that self-seeking is wrong and self-denial is merely nobler, but that the finding actually happens on the far side of the losing.

There is a corresponding softening of the finding promises into a general assurance that sincerity will be rewarded with whatever a man is looking for. Mat 7:7 is often quoted this way, detached from its object. But the passage is about asking the Father for good things, and the parallel in Luke names the gift explicitly: how much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him. The promise is not that every search succeeds; it is that this One, sought in this way, is found. Luke 15 then settles the matter of who does the finding, and it is worth noting that in all three parables the rejoicing belongs to the seeker, and heaven's joy is over one sinner that repenteth.
roots_summary: Hebrew mātsā' covers finding, attaining, and being sufficient. Greek heuriskō is to find or discover, and the compound aneuriskomai is to find after search, used of the shepherds finding Mary and Joseph and the babe.
roots_lines: Hebrew mātsā' (H4672) — to find, to attain, to come upon; some 456 occurrences, including Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD (Gen 6:8).
Hebrew chēn (H2580) — grace, favour; the object in the recurring idiom to find grace, which makes finding a matter of receiving rather than of earning.
Greek heuriskō (G2147) — to find, to discover, to obtain; some 176 occurrences, from the pearl of great price to the finding of the lost sheep.
Greek aneuriskomai (G429) — to find by search; used in Luk 2:16 of the shepherds and in Act 21:4 of finding out the disciples at Tyre.
Greek anapauō (G373) — to give rest; the object of the finding in Mat 11:29, ye shall find rest unto your souls, promised to those who take His yoke.
usage: Of the promised answer to prayer and search: seek, and ye shall find (Mat 7:7); those that seek me early shall find me (Pro 8:17).
Of divine recovery of the lost: I have found my sheep which was lost (Luk 15:6); come to seek and to save that which was lost (Luk 19:10).
Of the paradox of the lost and found life: whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it (Mat 16:25); happy is the man that findeth wisdom (Pro 3:13).

etymology: From Old English hīdan, to conceal, cognate with Greek keuthō — and unrelated to the other English hide, an animal skin, though both come down from the same distant root idea of covering. The Hebrew has several words with distinct flavours: chābā' is to hide oneself in fear, sāthar is to conceal or be secret (whence the secret place), and tsāphan is to hide by storing up, to treasure — which is the word behind hiding God's word in the heart.
biblical_def: Scripture uses hiding in three directions, and they must be kept apart. First, the creature hides from God, which is the immediate reflex of guilt: “Adam and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God amongst the trees of the garden” (Gen 3:8). It is futile — the LORD calls, Where art thou? — and every subsequent concealment of sin is a repetition of it, which is why the proverb says that he that covereth his sins shall not prosper, but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy. Second, God hides the believer, and this is pure mercy: “Thou art my hiding place; thou shalt preserve me from trouble; thou shalt compass me about with songs of deliverance” (Psa 32:7) — and it is worth noticing that this is the psalm of confessed sin, so the man who stopped hiding from God found a hiding place in Him. Isaiah gives the same shelter an eschatological form: “Come, my people, enter thou into thy chambers…hide thyself as it were for a little moment, until the indignation be overpast” (Isa 26:20). Paul states the settled position of the believer in this life: “ye are dead, and your life is hid with Christ in God” (Col 3:3) — hidden, and therefore safe, and therefore not yet visibly what it will be, for when Christ who is our life shall appear, then shall ye also appear with him in glory. Third, the believer hides God's word, storing it as treasure: “Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee” (Psa 119:11).
webster_summary: To conceal; in Scripture, the guilty creature's futile concealment from God, God's merciful concealment of His people in Himself, the believer's life hid with Christ in God, and the storing of God's word in the heart as treasure against sin.
webster_full: HIDE, v.t. 1. To conceal; to withhold or withdraw from sight; to place in any state or position in which the view is intercepted from the object.
2. To conceal from knowledge; to keep secret. Shall I hide from Abraham that thing which I do? Gen. 18.
3. To protect; to shelter. Thou art my hiding place. Psalm 32. Hide me under the shadow of thy wings. Psalm 17.
4. To treasure up; to lay up in store. Thy word have I hid in mine heart. Psalm 119.
5. To hide the face; when spoken of God, to withdraw the tokens of his favor; when spoken of men, to refuse to look upon, whether in shame or in contempt. Isa. 53; Isa. 59.
scriptures: Genesis 3:8
And they heard the voice of the LORD God walking in the garden in the cool of the day: and Adam and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God amongst the trees of the garden.
Psalm 32:7
Thou art my hiding place; thou shalt preserve me from trouble; thou shalt compass me about with songs of deliverance. Selah.
Colossians 3:3
For ye are dead, and your life is hid with Christ in God.
Psalm 119:11
Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee.
corruption_summary: The instinct to hide sin is now assisted by a culture of curated appearance, while the biblical remedy — confession to God and, where fitting, to men — is treated as unnecessary exposure rather than as the way out.
corruption_paragraphs: Concealment is the oldest post-fall reflex, and every age gives it new instruments. Adam had leaves and trees; the present age has a managed public self, edited and maintained, in which the gap between the presented life and the actual one can be held open indefinitely. The particular danger is that this feels like privacy rather than like hiding, and privacy is a real and legitimate good. The test is simple and Scripture supplies it: hiding that would be undone by confession is concealment of sin, and concealment of sin does not prosper. Psa 32 is the case history, written by a man who tried it — when I kept silence, my bones waxed old through my roaring all the day long — and who found relief only at the point of acknowledgment.

The opposite error deserves naming too, because the reaction against concealment has produced a compulsory openness in which every fault is published and nothing is kept. Scripture does not require this. Confession is directed — to God always, to the one wronged where there is a wrong, to the church where the matter is the church's — and love covereth a multitude of sins. Indiscriminate disclosure often serves the discloser and injures others, and it can coexist quite comfortably with impenitence. What Scripture asks is not exposure but honesty before God, and the promise attached to it is the one Psa 32 gives: blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered — covered, that is, by God, which is the only covering that works.
roots_summary: Hebrew distinguishes hiding in fear (chābā'), hiding as secrecy or shelter (sāthar), and hiding as treasuring up (tsāphan). Greek kruptō and its compounds cover concealment, with apokruptō for what God has hidden from the wise and revealed unto babes.
roots_lines: Hebrew chābā' (H2244) — to hide oneself, to withdraw in fear; the word of Adam among the trees and of Saul hidden among the stuff (1Sa 10:22).
Hebrew sāthar (H5641) — to hide, to conceal, to be secret; gives sēther, the secret place of Psa 91:1, and the phrase hide thy face.
Hebrew tsāphan (H6845) — to hide by storing, to treasure up; the verb of Psa 119:11, and of the goodness God has laid up for them that fear Him (Psa 31:19).
Greek kruptō (G2928) — to hide, conceal, keep secret; used of the treasure hid in a field and of the life hid with Christ in God (Col 3:3).
Greek apokruptō (G613) — to hide away, conceal from; used of things hid from the wise and prudent and revealed unto babes (Mat 11:25; Luk 10:21).
usage: Of guilty concealment: Adam and his wife hid themselves (Gen 3:8); he that covereth his sins shall not prosper (Pro 28:13).
Of divine shelter: thou art my hiding place (Psa 32:7); hide me under the shadow of thy wings (Psa 17:8); hide thyself until the indignation be overpast (Isa 26:20).
Of treasure and of present concealment in Christ: thy word have I hid in mine heart (Psa 119:11); your life is hid with Christ in God (Col 3:3).

etymology: From Old English leornian, to get knowledge, related to lāst, a track or footprint — to learn is to follow a trail. The Hebrew lāmad originally means to goad or train, as one trains a heifer to the yoke, and it gives talmīd, a disciple, and the later word Talmud. The Greek manthanō gives mathētēs, a disciple — a learner. The Bible's word for learning is therefore inseparable from its word for discipleship, and both carry the sense of being trained rather than merely informed.
biblical_def: Learning in Scripture is practical, personal, and often costly. It is practical because its object is conduct: “Learn to do well; seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow” (Isa 1:17) — a list of actions, addressed to a nation whose worship God had just refused. It is personal because its object is finally a Person rather than a subject: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart” (Mat 11:29). The figure is exact — a yoke is what a young beast is trained under, and the Lord offers His own, which is easy, and His burden, which is light, in place of the load the hearer is already carrying. It is costly because some lessons come only through experience: “I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content” (Php 4:11), written by a man in prison who had known both how to be abased and how to abound, and who says elsewhere that he learned it. And underneath all of it lies the necessity of divine teaching, without which nothing is truly learned at all: “It is written in the prophets, And they shall be all taught of God. Every man therefore that hath heard, and hath learned of the Father, cometh unto me” (Joh 6:45). The learning that ends in Christ is itself the Father's work; there is no coming to the Son except by it.
webster_summary: To gain knowledge or skill by instruction, training, or experience; in Scripture inseparable from discipleship, directed to conduct and to the Person of Christ, sometimes taught through affliction, and finally dependent on being taught of God.
webster_full: LEARN, v.t. 1. To gain knowledge of; to acquire knowledge or ideas of something before unknown.
2. To acquire skill in anything; to gain by practice a faculty of performing.
3. To teach; to communicate the knowledge of something before unknown. This use of the word is now obsolete in good writing, but occurs in the older versions and in common speech.
4. In Scripture, to learn of Christ is to become his disciple, taking his yoke and being trained under it. Matt. 11.
5. To learn by affliction; a frequent Scripture sense. Before I was afflicted I went astray, but now have I kept thy word. Psalm 119. He learned obedience by the things which he suffered. Heb. 5.
scriptures: Matthew 11:29
Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls.
Isaiah 1:17
Learn to do well; seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow.
Philippians 4:11
Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.
John 6:45
It is written in the prophets, And they shall be all taught of God. Every man therefore that hath heard, and hath learned of the Father, cometh unto me.
corruption_summary: Learning has been separated from obedience and from any master, so that it becomes the accumulation of information by an autonomous mind — the condition Paul describes as ever learning and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth.
corruption_paragraphs: The biblical learner is an apprentice under a master, and the biblical test of learning is what he can now do and has now become. Modern learning is largely the acquisition of information by a self-directing mind that submits to no one, and its test is what can be recalled or credentialled. The difference shows most sharply in what each does with a hard saying: the apprentice assumes the fault is his and stays under the yoke; the autonomous learner assumes the fault is the teacher's and moves on. Paul names the end state exactly — ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth — and it is worth noting that he is not describing the ignorant but the perpetually instructed.

There is a matching failure inside the church, where learning is set against doing as though depth of understanding excused delay in obedience. Isaiah writes to people who had the fullest possible liturgical education and whose new moons and appointed feasts God's soul hated; the remedy prescribed is not a further course of instruction but learn to do well, followed by five concrete duties toward the oppressed, the fatherless, and the widow. James says the same in his own idiom: be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves. The Lord's invitation holds both together and puts them in the right order — take my yoke upon you, and learn of me — the yoke first, and the learning under it.
roots_summary: Hebrew lāmad means to train or goad, and gives talmīd, a disciple. Greek manthanō gives mathētēs, disciple, and appears in the notable wordplay of Heb 5:8, He learned (emathen) obedience by the things which He suffered (epathen).
roots_lines: Hebrew lāmad (H3925) — to learn, to teach, to train; originally of goading cattle. Used in Psa 119:71, that I might learn thy statutes.
Hebrew talmīd (H8527) — a scholar, a disciple; occurring once, in 1Ch 25:8, of those taught in the songs of the LORD.
Greek manthanō (G3129) — to learn, to be instructed, to come to understand by practice; used of learning Christ (Eph 4:20) and learning contentment (Php 4:11).
Greek mathētēs (G3101) — a disciple, a learner; the standard New Testament name for a Christian in the Gospels and Acts, some 268 occurrences.
Greek paideuō (G3811) — to train a child, to instruct, to chastise; the word behind the discipline of Heb 12, in which the Father's correction is itself a form of teaching.
usage: Of learning conduct: learn to do well (Isa 1:17); learn first to shew piety at home (1Ti 5:4).
Of learning a Person: learn of me, for I am meek and lowly in heart (Mat 11:29); ye have not so learned Christ (Eph 4:20).

Of learning through affliction and of divine teaching: I have learned in whatsoever state I am (Php 4:11); he learned obedience by the things which he suffered (Heb 5:8); they shall be all taught of God (Joh 6:45).

etymology: From Old English standan, common Germanic, from an Indo-European root *stā- that runs through Latin stare and Greek histēmi and produces an enormous family in English — stable, statute, constant, substance, resist. The root sense is fixity, and every biblical use turns on it: what stands is what has not been moved, and the question in Scripture is always what holds a thing in place.
biblical_def: Standing in Scripture is a matter of position rather than of posture, and there are three great senses. First, standing before God, which is the question of acceptance: who shall stand in his holy place? — he that hath clean hands and a pure heart. The wicked shall not stand in the judgment, and the blessed man of the first psalm is defined partly by where he does not stand: “nor standeth in the way of sinners” (Psa 1:1). Second, standing firm against assault, which is the language of the Christian warfare. Paul's armour passage repeats the verb like a drumbeat: “take unto you the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand” (Eph 6:13) — and it is worth noting that no ground is to be gained, only held; the whole panoply is issued so that a man may still be on his feet when the day is over. Paul's shorter charge is to the same effect: “Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong” (1Co 16:13). Third, and underneath both, the standing that is not ours at all: “Nevertheless the foundation of God standeth sure, having this seal, The Lord knoweth them that are his” (2Ti 2:19). The believer is commanded to stand precisely because he is standing on something that cannot be moved; and the same apostle who says stand fast also says let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall, so that the command and the warning are held together by grace on both sides.
webster_summary: To be fixed in an upright position, and so in Scripture to be accepted before God, to hold ground against assault in the evil day, and to rest on the foundation of God which standeth sure — commanded of believers precisely because it is secured by God.
webster_full: STAND, v.i. 1. To be upon the feet, as an animal; not to sit, kneel or lie.
2. To be erect, supported by the roots, as a tree or plant.
3. To remain fixed or steady; to be firm; not to fall or be overthrown. The foundation of God standeth sure. 2 Tim. 2.
4. To be placed or situated with respect to acceptance; to be admitted into the presence of. Who shall stand in his holy place? Psalm 24.
5. To stand fast; to be fixed, immovable, and unshaken. Stand fast in the faith. 1 Cor. 16. To withstand; to hold out against assault. Eph. 6.
scriptures: Ephesians 6:13
Wherefore take unto you the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand.
1 Corinthians 16:13
Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong.
Psalm 1:1
Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful.
2 Timothy 2:19
Nevertheless the foundation of God standeth sure, having this seal, The Lord knoweth them that are his. And, Let every one that nameth the name of Christ depart from iniquity.
corruption_summary: Standing firm is recast as rigidity or as a failure of empathy, so that the one posture Scripture commands for the evil day is treated as a personality defect; and where it is retained, it is often detached from the armour that alone makes it possible.
corruption_paragraphs: The pressure on the Christian to yield is rarely argued now; it is applied through the vocabulary of manner. To hold a position is called rigidity, to decline a redefinition is called unkindness, and the whole apparatus of moral language is turned so that the man still standing appears to be the one doing harm. Eph 6 anticipates the shape of it exactly: the evil day is a day of assault, the enemies named are not flesh and blood, and the objective given is not advance but survival in position — having done all, to stand. Nothing in the passage licenses harshness; the armour includes the preparation of the gospel of peace, and the standing is done in truth and righteousness. But the passage does settle that yielding ground is defeat rather than maturity.

The opposite failure is to keep the word and lose the equipment. A man may resolve to stand fast and attempt it on temperament, conviction, or stubbornness, and Paul's point is that these will not hold in the evil day. Every piece named is either something God supplies or something God has done — His truth, His righteousness, His gospel, His word, and the shield of faith which is trust in Him — and the passage is bracketed by prayer, praying always with all prayer and supplication in the Spirit. The Reformed instinct here is important: 2Ti 2:19 puts the foundation under the standing, and the seal on it is the Lord knoweth them that are his, not they held out. Perseverance is genuine effort resting on a preservation that is God's.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'āmad is to stand, remain, endure; qūm is to arise or be established. Greek histēmi is to set or stand, stēkō a later form meaning to stand fast, and anthistēmi is to withstand.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'āmad (H5975) — to stand, to take one's stand, to endure; some 521 occurrences, from standing before the LORD to the sun standing still upon Gibeon.
Hebrew qūm (H6965) — to arise, stand up, be established; used of a word or counsel that shall stand, as in Isa 40:8, the word of our God shall stand for ever.
Greek histēmi (G2476) — to set, place, stand; used of standing before the judgment seat and of the foundation that standeth sure.
Greek stēkō (G4739) — to stand fast, persevere; a later form derived from the perfect of histēmi, used in 1Co 16:13 and Php 1:27, stand fast in one spirit.
Greek anthistēmi (G436) — to set against, withstand, resist; used in Eph 6:13 and in Jas 4:7, resist the devil, and he will flee from you.
usage: Of acceptance before God: who shall stand in his holy place? (Psa 24:3); the ungodly shall not stand in the judgment (Psa 1:5).
Of holding ground in conflict: having done all, to stand (Eph 6:13); stand fast in the faith (1Co 16:13); stand fast in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free (Gal 5:1).
Of what stands independently of us: the foundation of God standeth sure (2Ti 2:19); the word of our God shall stand for ever (Isa 40:8).

etymology: From Old English sittan, common Germanic, from the Indo-European root *sed- — the same root behind Latin sedere and the English words seat, session, see (a bishop's), and settle. The Hebrew yāshab means both to sit and to dwell or remain, and that double sense governs much of its biblical use: to sit somewhere is to take up residence there, which is why sitting in the seat of the scornful is a matter of settled company rather than a passing posture.
biblical_def: Sitting in Scripture signifies settled position, completed work, and authority to judge. Its highest use is Christological. “The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool” (Psa 110:1) is the Old Testament verse most quoted in the New, and the session of Christ — His sitting down at the right hand of the Majesty on high — is the great proof that the sacrificial work is finished, since the Levitical priests stood daily ministering and offering the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins, but this man, after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down. A seated priest is a finished atonement. Union with Christ then extends the posture to His people: God “hath raised us up together, and made us sit together in heavenly places in Christ Jesus” (Eph 2:6), a present standing rather than a future hope, and the promise to the overcomer is the same, “To him that overcometh will I grant to sit with me in my throne” (Rev 3:21). Sitting is also the posture of the learner at a teacher's feet — Mary “sat at Jesus' feet, and heard his word” (Luk 10:39), and was told she had chosen the good part, which shall not be taken away from her. And it can mark the settled company of the wicked, the third and worst stage of the first psalm's descent: walking in the counsel of the ungodly, standing in the way of sinners, and finally sitting in the seat of the scornful.
webster_summary: To rest on the lower part of the body, and in Scripture to be settled, enthroned, or at rest from finished work; the posture of Christ's session at the right hand, of the believer seated in heavenly places in Him, of the disciple at the Master's feet, and of settled company good or evil.
webster_full: SIT, v.i. 1. To rest upon the buttocks, as animals; to be seated.
2. To rest; to remain; to abide; in which sense the Hebrew word is rendered both to sit and to dwell.
3. To be placed in the seat of authority; to be in a state of rest or of judgment. Sit thou at my right hand. Psalm 110. When the Son of man shall sit in the throne of his glory. Matt. 25.
4. To be in the posture of a learner. Mary sat at Jesus' feet and heard his word. Luke 10. Paul was brought up at the feet of Gamaliel. Acts 22.
5. To sit down; to begin a siege, or to settle in a place. To sit in the seat of the scornful; to take one's settled place among mockers. Psalm 1.
scriptures: Psalm 110:1
A Psalm of David. The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool.
Ephesians 2:6
And hath raised us up together, and made us sit together in heavenly places in Christ Jesus:
Luke 10:39
And she had a sister called Mary, which also sat at Jesus' feet, and heard his word.
Revelation 3:21
To him that overcometh will I grant to sit with me in my throne, even as I also overcame, and am set down with my Father in his throne.
corruption_summary: The session of Christ is the most neglected article of the creed in ordinary preaching, so that the finished, reigning, interceding Lord is replaced by a Saviour still pleading and a church still trying to secure what He has already obtained.
corruption_paragraphs: Christ's sitting down is doctrine, not scenery, and Hebrews argues from the posture itself. Every priest standeth daily ministering and offering oftentimes the same sacrifices which can never take away sins; but this man, after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God. The standing priest signifies unfinished work; the seated priest signifies a work that cannot be added to. Where the session is neglected, two errors move in. Rome's mass re-presents an offering that Scripture says was made once; and much popular evangelicalism, though it denies any repeated sacrifice, preaches an anxious Christ whose success depends on the response He is given, which quietly undoes the same finality.

The corresponding loss on the believer's side is Eph 2:6. The apostle says God hath made us sit together in heavenly places in Christ — a completed action describing a present position — and this is the foundation for everything he commands in the second half of the letter, including the standing of Eph 6. To treat the Christian's seat in Christ as a future reward that present performance might yet forfeit is to reverse the order of the epistle and to put the believer back on his own footing. The right response is neither presumption nor anxiety but the one the same apostle draws: if ye then be risen with Christ, seek those things which are above, where Christ sitteth on the right hand of God.
roots_summary: Hebrew yāshab means to sit, dwell, or remain, and is used of God who sitteth in the heavens and of Israel dwelling in the land. Greek distinguishes kathizō, to take a seat, from kathēmai, to be seated; sugkathizō is to be seated together, used in Eph 2:6.
roots_lines: Hebrew yāshab (H3427) — to sit, remain, dwell, inhabit; over 1,000 occurrences, covering both posture and settled residence.
Hebrew k'sē' (H3678) — a seat, a throne; the word behind the throne of grace and the throne of judgment.
Greek kathēmai (G2521) — to be seated, to dwell; used of Him that sitteth on the throne throughout Revelation.
Greek kathizō (G2523) — to cause to sit, to sit down; used in Heb 10:12 of the one offering after which He sat down, and in Heb 1:3 of the session on high.
Greek sugkathizō (G4776) — to seat together with; used in Eph 2:6 of believers made to sit together in heavenly places in Christ Jesus.
usage: Of the session and reign of Christ: sit thou at my right hand (Psa 110:1); he sat down on the right hand of God (Heb 10:12).
Of the believer's position and prospect: made us sit together in heavenly places (Eph 2:6); to sit with me in my throne (Rev 3:21).
Of the disciple and of settled company: Mary sat at Jesus' feet (Luk 10:39); nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful (Psa 1:1).

pos: n. and v. (rendering Hebrew shēnâh, yāshēn, and Greek hupnos, koimaō)
etymology: From Old English slāp, common West Germanic, from a root meaning to be slack or limp — sleep named for the loosening of the body. The Greek koimaō, to put to sleep, is the source of English cemetery, which is literally a sleeping-place; the early Christians named their burial grounds from the New Testament's habit of calling the death of believers sleep, and the name preaches the resurrection every time it is used.
biblical_def: Sleep in Scripture is first a gift and a mark of trust. “It is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late, to eat the bread of sorrows: for so he giveth his beloved sleep” (Psa 127:2) — the anxious overwork of the man who thinks the house depends on him is set against a sleep God gives. The Lord Jesus asleep on a pillow in the hinder part of the ship, in a storm that terrified professional fishermen (Mar 4:38), is the picture of that trust in its perfection, and the disciples' question — carest thou not that we perish? — is the ordinary unbelief that mistakes His rest for indifference. Second, sleep is the standing figure for sloth and its slow ruin: “Yet a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep” (Pro 6:10), and poverty comes as one that travelleth. The New Testament turns the same figure on spiritual drowsiness — it is high time to awake out of sleep; awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead. Third and most consequentially, sleep is the New Testament's tender word for the death of believers: “them also which sleep in Jesus will God bring with him” (1Th 4:14). The word is chosen deliberately, because sleep is temporary, restful, and ends in waking; it is never used to suggest that the dead are unconscious of Christ, for to be absent from the body is to be present with the Lord.
webster_summary: The natural rest of the body, given by God to His beloved and refused by the anxious; in Scripture also the figure of sloth and of spiritual drowsiness, and the New Testament's chosen word for the death of believers, who sleep in Jesus and shall be brought with Him.
webster_full: SLEEP, n. That state of an animal in which the voluntary exertion of his mental and corporeal powers is suspended, and he rests unconscious of what passes around him.
2. In Scripture, a gift of God to his people. He giveth his beloved sleep. Psalm 127. I laid me down and slept; I awaked, for the LORD sustained me. Psalm 3.
3. Sloth; indolence; the state of the sluggard. Love not sleep, lest thou come to poverty. Prov. 20.
4. Spiritual insensibility; a state of security and inattention to the concerns of the soul. Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead. Eph. 5.
5. Death; the repose of the body in the grave, so called in the New Testament because it is temporary and shall end in the resurrection. Them which sleep in Jesus. 1 Thess. 4.
scriptures: Psalm 127:2
It is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late, to eat the bread of sorrows: for so he giveth his beloved sleep.
Proverbs 6:10
Yet a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep:
Mark 4:38
And he was in the hinder part of the ship, asleep on a pillow: and they awake him, and say unto him, Master, carest thou not that we perish?
1 Thessalonians 4:14
For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so them also which sleep in Jesus will God bring with him.
corruption_summary: The New Testament's figure of sleep for the believer's death has been pressed into the doctrine of soul sleep — an unconscious interval between death and resurrection — which contradicts the passages that place the departed believer consciously with Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Soul sleep reasons from a figure of speech to a state of being. Because the New Testament calls the death of believers sleep, it is argued that the soul is unconscious until the resurrection. But the figure is chosen for what is obvious about sleep to onlookers — the body lies still, the condition is temporary, and it ends in waking — and it describes the body, which is what onlookers see. The direct statements about the departed run the other way. Paul desires to depart and to be with Christ, which is far better, a preference that makes no sense if death is an unconscious gap; to be absent from the body is to be present with the Lord; the Lord told the thief, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise; and the souls under the altar in Rev 6 speak. The Reformed confession holds both: the souls of the righteous are received into the highest heavens at death, while their bodies rest in their graves until the resurrection.

A quieter corruption is the treatment of sleep itself as wasted time, a weakness to be minimised by discipline or chemistry. Psa 127 speaks directly to this and calls the round of early rising and late sitting-up the bread of sorrows, contrasting it with sleep that God gives to His beloved. To sleep is to lay down, for a third of one's life, all control over one's affairs, and to do so nightly is a repeated practical confession that the LORD keeps the city and that He who keeps Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep. Scripture does condemn the sluggard, and sharply; but the sin there is the love of ease, not the acceptance of a creaturely limit.
roots_summary: Hebrew shēnâh is sleep and yāshēn to sleep; tardēmâh is the deep sleep God caused to fall on Adam and on Abram. Greek hupnos is ordinary sleep, while koimaō is the verb used of believers who have fallen asleep in death.
roots_lines: Hebrew shēnâh (H8142) — sleep; used in Psa 127:2, so he giveth his beloved sleep, and in Pro 6:4, give not sleep to thine eyes.
Hebrew tardēmâh (H8639) — a deep sleep, a trance; the sleep that fell on Adam (Gen 2:21), on Abram (Gen 15:12), and on Saul's camp (1Sa 26:12).
Greek hupnos (G5258) — sleep; used literally, and figuratively in Rom 13:11, now it is high time to awake out of sleep.
Greek koimaō (G2837) — to put to sleep, and in the passive to fall asleep, that is, to die; the word in 1Th 4:14 and 1Co 15:20, Christ the firstfruits of them that slept.
Greek koimētērion — a sleeping place; the term from which cemetery derives, adopted by the early church for its burial grounds as a confession of the resurrection.
usage: Of God's gift and the believer's rest: he giveth his beloved sleep (Psa 127:2); I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep (Psa 4:8); Christ asleep in the storm (Mar 4:38).
Of sloth: a little sleep, a little slumber (Pro 6:10); love not sleep, lest thou come to poverty (Pro 20:13).
Of death and of spiritual drowsiness: them which sleep in Jesus (1Th 4:14); awake thou that sleepest (Eph 5:14); our friend Lazarus sleepeth (Joh 11:11).

pos: n. and v. (rendering Hebrew tsārâh and 'ākar, and Greek thlipsis, tarassō)
etymology: From Old French trubler, ultimately from Latin turbidus, disturbed, muddied — the image is of clear water stirred up and made turbid. The Hebrew tsārâh comes from a root meaning narrow or straitened, so that trouble is pictured as a tight place, a constriction; and the Greek thlipsis is literally pressure, a pressing or squeezing. Between them the two languages give trouble two faces: it muddies, and it presses.
biblical_def: Scripture treats trouble as the settled condition of life under the curse rather than as an interruption of a normal calm. Job states it flatly: “Man that is born of a woman is of few days, and full of trouble” (Job 14:1). The Lord Jesus is equally plain and adds the remedy in the same breath: “In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world” (Joh 16:33) — the promise is not exemption but a conquered world and a cheerful heart within it. Because trouble is expected, the psalms do not treat it as evidence against God's care; they make it the occasion of His nearness: “God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble” (Psa 46:1) — and the adjective matters, since the help is present rather than eventual. The same psalm draws the conclusion Scripture always draws from it: therefore will not we fear, though the earth be removed. The Lord's own word to troubled disciples is a command about the heart with a prescribed cure: “Let not your heart be troubled: ye believe in God, believe also in me” (Joh 14:1) — the disturbance is to be answered by an act of faith in a Person, not by a change of circumstances, and He goes on to speak of the Father's house and of His coming again. Scripture also knows a trouble that men bring on themselves and others: Achan troubled Israel, and the valley of Achor is named for it.
webster_summary: Distress, affliction, and pressure; in Scripture the ordinary condition of man under the curse and of the believer in the world, met not by exemption but by a very present help, an overcoming Lord, and a heart commanded to rest in Him.
webster_full: TROUBLE, v.t. 1. To agitate; to disturb; to put into confused motion, as water. An angel went down and troubled the water. John 5.
2. To disturb; to perplex; to afflict; to grieve; to vex. Let not your heart be troubled. John 14.
3. To busy; to give occasion for labor; as, I will not trouble you further.
4. TROUBLE, n. Disturbance of mind; agitation; affliction; distress. Man is born unto trouble, as the sparks fly upward. Job 5.

5. In Scripture, the word answers to a Hebrew term signifying a strait or narrow place, and to a Greek term signifying pressure; whence God is said to set our feet in a large room, and to deliver out of straits.
scriptures: Job 14:1
Man that is born of a woman is of few days, and full of trouble.
Psalm 46:1
To the chief Musician for the sons of Korah, A Song upon Alamoth. God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.
John 14:1
Let not your heart be troubled: ye believe in God, believe also in me.
John 16:33
These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.
corruption_summary: Two teachings share one error about trouble: the prosperity gospel says the believer should not have it, and a therapeutic Christianity says its only meaning is what it does for personal growth — both losing the biblical account of affliction as appointed, purposeful, and accompanied.
corruption_paragraphs: The prosperity teaching treats trouble as evidence of insufficient faith, so that the afflicted Christian is doubly burdened — by the affliction and by the verdict that he brought it on himself. Scripture forecloses this. The Lord promised tribulation in the world as a matter of course; Paul's résumé is stripes, prisons, shipwrecks, and a thorn in the flesh that was not removed after three requests; and Peter tells his readers not to think it strange concerning the fiery trial, as though some strange thing happened unto them. The doctrine of providence is the honest alternative: all things work together for good to them that love God, which is a promise about outcome under God's hand, not a promise of an untroubled passage.

The therapeutic misreading is gentler and now more common. It keeps trouble but reduces its meaning to personal growth, so that affliction is valuable insofar as it makes one stronger or more self-aware, and God is the facilitator of that development. Scripture's account is larger and less flattering. Affliction is chastening from a Father to sons, working the peaceable fruit of righteousness; it is fellowship with Christ's sufferings; it equips us to comfort others with the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted; and it is producing a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory. Above all it is accompanied — when thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee — and the presence, not the lesson, is the promise the psalms rest on.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsārâh pictures trouble as a narrow, straitened place, from tsārar, to bind or cramp; 'ākar is to trouble in the sense of stirring up and bringing disaster, as Achan did. Greek thlipsis is pressure, and tarassō is to agitate as water is stirred.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsārâh (H6869) — distress, straits, trouble; from tsārar, to be narrow. The word in Psa 46:1 and in Jacob's trouble (Jer 30:7).
Hebrew 'ākar (H5916) — to trouble, to stir up, to bring disaster; used of Achan, and giving the name of the valley of Achor (Jos 7:25-26).
Hebrew 'āmāl (H5999) — toil, mischief, sorrow; often rendered trouble, as in Psa 73:5, they are not in trouble as other men.
Greek thlipsis (G2347) — pressure, affliction, tribulation; some 45 occurrences, from the tribulation of Joh 16:33 to the great tribulation of Rev 7:14.
Greek tarassō (G5015) — to agitate, stir, disturb; used of the troubled water at Bethesda, of Herod troubled at the wise men, and of the heart in Joh 14:1.
usage: Of the human condition: man that is born of a woman is full of trouble (Job 14:1); man is born unto trouble, as the sparks fly upward (Job 5:7).
Of God's help within it: a very present help in trouble (Psa 46:1); call upon me in the day of trouble: I will deliver thee (Psa 50:15).
Of the commanded heart and the overcoming Lord: let not your heart be troubled (Joh 14:1); in the world ye shall have tribulation (Joh 16:33).
